statement: The Standards review axis asks whether the code conforms to the repository's documented coding standards.
trigger: a diff is being reviewed
outcome: a Standards-axis assessment is produced
notes: One of the two named review axes.
rationale: Defines what the Standards axis judges; needed only while that sub-review runs, not a standalone checkpoint or reusable outcome by itself.
alternatives_considered: separate workflow per axis
AGENTS.md invariant

statement: The Spec review axis asks whether the code faithfully implements the originating issue, PRD, or spec.
trigger: a diff is being reviewed
outcome: a Spec-axis assessment is produced
notes: The second named review axis.
rationale: Defines what the Spec axis judges; scoped to that sub-review, not an independent checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: separate workflow per axis
AGENTS.md invariant

statement: The Standards and Spec reviews run as parallel, isolated sub-agents so neither review's context pollutes the other, and this skill aggregates both sets of findings afterward.
trigger: both review sources are identified
outcome: two independent review passes are produced and later merged into one report
notes: Core reason the two axes are executed as separate fresh contexts rather than one pass.
rationale: This is a durable checkpoint boundary: whether the reviews are context-isolated changes what evidence a fresh execution starts from, and operators would care whether it ran isolated or not.
alternatives_considered: single-agent sequential review (rejected: risks cross-axis contamination)

statement: The review's fixed comparison point is whatever the user specified (commit SHA, branch, tag, HEAD~N, etc); if the user did not specify one, the actor must ask for it before proceeding.

source.locator: Step 1: Pin the fixed point, lines 19-19

trigger: user requests a review without naming a comparison point
outcome: the actor asks the user for the fixed point rather than guessing
notes: Judgment/consent checkpoint — the actor must not invent a comparison point.
rationale: Requires the actor to recognize missing input and ask, which is a judgment call inside the first stage, not a separate reusable workflow.
alternatives_considered: silently default to a fixed point (rejected: could review the wrong range)

statement: The comparison diff is captured once as the three-dot form `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (so the comparison is against the merge-base), alongside the commit list via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

source.locator: Step 1: Pin the fixed point, lines 21-21

trigger: the fixed point has been established
outcome: a stable diff and commit list exist for both sub-agents to consume
notes: Deterministic mechanics for producing the review's input; the three-dot-vs-two-dot choice is a specific, load-bearing detail.
rationale: Repeatable, deterministic git invocation whose outcome (the diff/commit-list content) is subordinate to the pin-fixed-point checkpoint, not itself a durable checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: two-dot diff (rejected: compares against fixed-point's tip, not merge-base)

statement: Before spawning the two parallel review sub-agents, the actor must confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse`) and the diff is non-empty; a bad ref or empty diff must fail at this point, not inside the sub-agents.

source.locator: Step 1: Pin the fixed point, lines 23-23

trigger: the fixed point and diff command are captured
outcome: invalid input is caught before expensive parallel work starts
notes: Explicit fail-fast rule: validation must happen before fan-out, not be discovered independently by both sub-agents.
rationale: A meaningful durable checkpoint: whether validation happened before or after fan-out changes failure cost and where the process reports the failure.
alternatives_considered: let each sub-agent independently validate (rejected explicitly by the source: 'not inside two parallel sub-agents')

statement: The spec source for the Spec axis is located in a fixed priority order: issue references in commit messages, then a path the user passed as an argument, then a PRD/spec file under docs/, specs/, or .scratch/ matching the branch or feature name, then — if nothing is found — asking the user; if the user says no spec exists, the Spec sub-agent is skipped and reports 'no spec available'.

source.locator: Step 2: Identify the spec source, lines 27-32

trigger: identifying what the Spec axis should compare against
outcome: a spec source is found, or the Spec review is explicitly skipped with a reason
notes: A precise fallback ladder; each rung is a distinct resolution strategy.
rationale: This is context/procedure for one stage (locating the spec) with judgment at the final 'ask the user' rung; not a durable checkpoint on its own since it's subordinate to preparing the Spec sub-agent's input.
alternatives_considered: always require the user to supply the spec (rejected: too much friction when it's discoverable)
AGENTS.md invariant

statement: The Standards axis always carries a fixed baseline set of Fowler code smells (Refactoring, ch. 3) in addition to whatever standards the repository documents itself, so the Standards review has content even when the repository documents nothing.

source.locator: Step 3: Identify the standards sources, lines 38-38

trigger: reviewing the Standards axis
outcome: a non-empty standards basis exists for the Standards sub-agent even in an undocumented repo
notes: Establishes that the smell baseline is a fallback content source, always present.
rationale: This is reusable reference content (the smell baseline) supplied to a stage's actor, not itself a checkpoint; candidate for a shared context if other review-like workflows need the same baseline.
alternatives_considered: require repo-documented standards only (rejected: leaves undocumented repos with no basis)

statement: A documented repository standard always overrides the smell baseline: where the repo's own standard endorses something the baseline would flag, the smell is suppressed.

source.locator: Step 3: Identify the standards sources, lines 40-40

trigger: a baseline smell conflicts with a repo-documented standard
outcome: the repo's documented standard wins and the smell is suppressed
notes: A precedence rule between two content sources.
rationale: Precedence rule scoped to the Standards sub-review's judgment, not an independent checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: treat baseline and repo standards as equally weighted (rejected explicitly)

statement: Every baseline smell is a labelled judgment-call heuristic, never a hard violation, and the reviewer must skip anything tooling already enforces.

source.locator: Step 3: Identify the standards sources, lines 41-41

trigger: applying the smell baseline
outcome: smells are reported as judgment calls, not hard failures; tooling-enforced items are not repeated
notes: Severity/confidence framing rule for the baseline.
rationale: Governs how findings from the shared baseline are framed within the Standards stage; not a standalone checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: treat smells as hard violations (rejected explicitly)

statement: The fixed smell baseline names twelve heuristics (Mysterious Name, Duplicated Code, Feature Envy, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession, Repeated Switches, Shotgun Surgery, Divergent Change, Speculative Generality, Message Chains, Middle Man, Refused Bequest), each with a 'what it is' description and a 'how to fix' pointer, to match against the diff.
trigger: applying the smell baseline to a diff
outcome: each matched smell is named with its corresponding fix direction
notes: The baseline content itself; reused verbatim by the review actor. Verbatim reference content, high reuse potential across any future standards-review workflow.
rationale: This is deterministic reference content (a checklist) invoked while crossing the Standards checkpoint — a candidate shared helper/context if other workflows also need a code-smell baseline.
alternatives_considered: inline duplicate copies per workflow (rejected: single source of truth preferred)

statement: Both review sub-agents are spawned together in a single message using two parallel general-purpose Agent tool calls.
trigger: spec source and standards sources are both identified
outcome: two isolated sub-agent executions run concurrently
notes: Mechanism detail (single-message dual-spawn) but load-bearing for the isolation guarantee in CR03.
rationale: Deterministic invocation mechanics subordinate to the parallel-review checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: spawn sequentially (rejected: defeats the isolation purpose, and is slower)

statement: The Standards sub-agent's prompt must include the diff command and commit list, the located standards-source files plus the full smell baseline pasted in (since the sub-agent has no other access to it), and a brief asking it to report per-file/hunk hard standard violations (cited to the standard) and baseline smells (named and quoted), distinguishing hard violations from judgment calls, skipping tooling-enforced items, under 400 words.
trigger: spawning the Standards sub-agent
outcome: the sub-agent has everything needed to produce a bounded, well-formed Standards report
notes: Specifies the exact contract for one sub-agent's input and output shape.
rationale: This is the actor-context needed to run the Standards sub-review; the sub-agent needs judgment to distinguish hard violations from judgment calls.
alternatives_considered: let the sub-agent look up the baseline itself (rejected: sub-agent has no other access to it, so it must be pasted in)

statement: The Spec sub-agent's prompt must include the diff command and commit list, the path or fetched contents of the spec, and a brief asking it to report missing/partial requirements, scope creep (unasked-for behavior), and requirements that look implemented but wrong, quoting the spec line for each finding, under 400 words.
trigger: spawning the Spec sub-agent
outcome: the sub-agent has everything needed to produce a bounded, well-formed Spec report
notes: Specifies the exact contract for the other sub-agent's input and output shape.
rationale: Actor-context for the Spec sub-review, requiring judgment to classify findings into missing/scope-creep/wrong-implementation.
alternatives_considered: skip spec-line citation (rejected: findings must be traceable to the spec text)

statement: If no spec is found, the Spec sub-agent is skipped entirely and the final report notes this explicitly.
trigger: no spec source was located in Step 2
outcome: the Spec axis is honestly reported as unavailable rather than fabricated
notes: Graceful-degradation rule tied to CR07's fallback ladder.
rationale: Conditional branch inside the synthesize/aggregate step, not an independent checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: invent a spec review anyway (rejected: would fabricate findings against nothing)

statement: The two sub-agent reports are presented under separate `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned, and must never be merged or reranked against each other since the two axes are deliberately kept separate.
trigger: both sub-agent reports have returned
outcome: a combined report exists with the two axes still clearly distinguishable
notes: The core output-shape rule and the anti-merging rule that protects the two-axis design.
rationale: A durable checkpoint: whether the two axes stayed separated or got merged is exactly the kind of outcome an operator or later reviewer would care about and want to verify independently.
alternatives_considered: merge/rerank into one combined finding list (rejected explicitly — see 'Why two axes')

statement: The aggregated report ends with a one-line summary of total findings per axis and the worst issue within each axis, without picking one overall winner across axes.
trigger: the two-axis report has been assembled
outcome: a concise cross-cutting summary line closes the report, without collapsing the two axes into one ranking
notes: Precise closing-format rule.
rationale: Format detail of the aggregate stage's output, not a separate checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: rank findings globally across axes (rejected: reintroduces the masking the separation prevents)

statement: The two-axis design exists because a change can pass one axis and fail the other (standards-compliant but spec-wrong, or spec-correct but convention-breaking), and reporting them separately stops either axis from masking the other's failure.
trigger: n/a (design rationale)
outcome: the two-axis structure is preserved rather than collapsed
notes: This is rationale/justification rather than an operational step; informs why CR03/CR16 exist.
rationale: Rationale supporting the separation invariant already captured operationally in CR03/CR16; not independently actionable.
alternatives_considered: treat as a stable operating invariant instead (considered, but it is scoped to this one workflow's design, not a repo-wide rule)

statement: The diagnosing-bugs workflow triggers when the user says 'diagnose'/'debug this', or reports something broken, throwing, failing, or slow, and phases may be skipped only when explicitly justified.
trigger: user reports a defect or performance regression, or asks to diagnose/debug
outcome: the diagnosis-loop workflow is entered
notes: Entry trigger and the 'skip only with justification' discipline rule for the whole workflow.
rationale: Recognizable trigger, bounded outcome (root cause found and fixed with regression coverage), and completion condition — matches the §6.2 workflow test directly.
alternatives_considered: treat as a stage inside a larger 'implement' workflow (rejected: it is independently invocable and has its own trigger)

statement: Before diagnosing, the actor should read CONTEXT.md (if it exists) for the relevant modules' mental model and check ADRs in the area being touched.
trigger: beginning to explore the codebase for a bug
outcome: the actor has domain vocabulary and prior architectural decisions before hypothesizing
notes: Cross-cutting context-loading rule shared in spirit with tdd/SKILL.md's identical CONTEXT.md instruction.
rationale: References a shared, workflow-external artifact (CONTEXT.md/ADRs) used the same way by tdd/SKILL.md — candidate for a shared context convention rather than a workflow-local one.
alternatives_considered: workflow-local instruction only (rejected: identical wording appears in the tdd skill, suggesting a shared convention)

statement: A tight pass/fail signal that goes red specifically on the bug in question is the entire skill; with it, bisection/hypothesis-testing/instrumentation all just consume it, and without it no code-reading will substitute.
trigger: starting Phase 1 (build a feedback loop)
outcome: the actor commits to building a red-capable loop before any hypothesis work
notes: The stated central thesis of the whole skill.
rationale: This is the guiding principle inside the first stage, not a separate checkpoint; the checkpoint itself is 'a tight loop exists', captured separately in DB11.
alternatives_considered: treat as a stable operating invariant (considered, but it is diagnosis-specific, not broadly applicable outside this workflow)

statement: Disproportionate effort should be spent building the feedback loop; the actor should be aggressive, creative, and refuse to give up at this stage.
trigger: building the feedback loop
outcome: effort is weighted toward loop construction over premature hypothesizing
notes: Effort-allocation directive.
rationale: Behavioral guidance for how the actor should operate inside the stage, not itself a checkpoint.

statement: Feedback loops should be attempted in roughly this priority order: a failing test at the seam that reaches the bug; a curl/HTTP script against a running dev server; a CLI invocation diffed against a known-good snapshot; a headless-browser script (Playwright/Puppeteer); replaying a captured trace; a throwaway minimal harness; a property/fuzz loop for 'sometimes wrong output' bugs; a bisection harness automatable via `git bisect run`; a differential loop comparing old vs new versions or configs.
trigger: no feedback loop exists yet
outcome: the actor selects a construction strategy from a ranked menu rather than inventing one ad hoc
notes: The nine primary strategies, ordered by preference.
rationale: A ranked decision menu the actor applies with judgment (choosing the best-fit strategy for the bug at hand) inside the first stage.
alternatives_considered: a single fixed method (rejected: different bug shapes need different loop types)

statement: As a last resort, when a human must click through the UI, the actor drives them through a structured human-in-the-loop Bash script (`scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`) so even a human-in-the-loop repro stays structured, and the captured output feeds back to the actor.
trigger: no automatable loop is possible and a human must operate the UI
outcome: a structured HITL script captures the human's observations for the actor to consume
notes: This is the one loop-construction rung that requires an external deterministic helper script; the script itself (`scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`) is disposition helper-evidence, not separately decomposed, but the rule to invoke it as a copy-and-edit template is the durable behavior.
rationale: Deterministic machinery (a copy-and-edit prompt/capture Bash template) invoked as a last-resort mechanism while crossing the feedback-loop checkpoint; the durable intent is 'structure the human-in-the-loop capture', independent of it being a Bash script specifically.
alternatives_considered: skip HITL entirely and always demand an automatable loop (rejected: some bugs genuinely require a human click)

statement: Once a loop exists it should be tightened by asking whether it can be made faster (cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow scope), sharper (assert on the specific symptom, not merely 'didn't crash'), and more deterministic (pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network).
trigger: a feedback loop exists but is slow/vague/flaky
outcome: the loop is iteratively improved along three named axes before being relied upon
notes: Three concrete tightening axes.
rationale: Iteration guidance within the feedback-loop stage; not itself a new checkpoint.

statement: A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic loop is treated as a debugging superpower.
trigger: evaluating loop quality
outcome: loop quality is judged against a concrete speed/determinism bar
notes: Illustrative quality bar reinforcing DB07.
rationale: Supporting rationale for the tightening rule, not independently actionable.

statement: For non-deterministic bugs the goal is a higher reproduction rate, not a clean repro: loop the trigger ~100x, parallelize, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps; a 50%-flake bug is debuggable, a 1% one is not, so the actor keeps raising the rate until it is debuggable.
trigger: the bug does not reproduce deterministically
outcome: the actor drives reproduction rate up until the bug is debuggable, rather than treating flakiness as a dead end
notes: A specific technique branch for flaky bugs, with a quantified debuggability threshold.
rationale: Conditional technique inside the feedback-loop stage for a specific bug shape.

statement: If no loop can genuinely be built, the actor must stop and say so explicitly, list what was tried, and ask the user for environment access, a captured artifact (HAR, log dump, core dump, timestamped screen recording), or permission to add temporary production instrumentation — and must not proceed to hypothesize without a loop.

source.locator: Phase 1: When you genuinely cannot build a loop, lines 49-49

trigger: every loop-construction attempt has failed
outcome: the actor escalates to the user with a specific, bounded ask instead of guessing
notes: A hard stop-and-escalate rule with a fixed menu of asks; explicitly forbids skipping ahead.
rationale: Judgment-requiring escalation branch of the feedback-loop stage — the actor must recognize failure and choose among named escalation options.
alternatives_considered: silently proceed to hypothesize without a loop (rejected explicitly by the source)

statement: Phase 1 is complete only when the actor can name one already-run command (script path, test invocation, curl) that is red-capable (drives the actual bug path and asserts the user's exact symptom), deterministic (or, for flaky bugs, a pinned high reproduction rate), fast (seconds not minutes), and agent-runnable (unattended, human only via the HITL script).
trigger: the actor believes a feedback loop is ready
outcome: phase completion is judged against four explicit, checkable criteria rather than a vibe
notes: The formal exit criterion for the first checkpoint — a checklist, not prose.
rationale: This is the meaningful durable checkpoint itself: whether the loop meets this four-point bar is exactly the kind of state an operator would want measured and would block progression on.
alternatives_considered: treat any loop as sufficient once it exists (rejected: the criteria are explicit and checked)

statement: If the actor catches themselves reading code to build a theory before the red-capable command exists, that is the exact failure the skill prevents, and no red-capable command means no Phase 2.
trigger: the actor is tempted to hypothesize before Phase 1 completes
outcome: the actor stops and returns to loop-building instead of hypothesizing early
notes: A hard gate preventing phase-skipping.
rationale: This is the transition gate between stage 10 and stage 20 — a durable checkpoint enforcing ordering.
alternatives_considered: allow early hypothesizing if the actor feels confident (rejected explicitly)

statement: Phase 2 begins by running the loop and watching it go red, confirming the bug appears.
trigger: Phase 1's completion criterion is met
outcome: the bug is confirmed to reproduce via the built loop
notes: Entry action of the Reproduce+Minimize stage.
rationale: Marks entry into the second durable checkpoint of the workflow.

statement: The actor must confirm the loop reproduces the specific failure mode the user described (not a coincidentally nearby different failure), that it reproduces across multiple runs (or at a high enough rate for non-deterministic bugs), and that the exact symptom has been captured for later verification.
trigger: the loop has gone red
outcome: the reproduction is confirmed to be the right bug, not a look-alike
notes: A three-item verification checklist guarding against 'wrong bug, wrong fix'.
rationale: Judgment checklist inside the reproduce-minimize stage.

statement: Once red, the repro is shrunk to the smallest scenario that still goes red by cutting inputs, callers, config, data, and steps one at a time, re-running the loop after each cut, keeping only what is load-bearing for the failure.
trigger: the bug reliably reproduces
outcome: a minimal repro is produced containing only load-bearing elements
notes: The minimization algorithm: one-cut-at-a-time with re-verification.
rationale: Deterministic-ish iterative procedure inside the reproduce-minimize stage; still requires judgment about what to cut.

statement: Minimizing the repro shrinks the hypothesis space for Phase 3 and produces the clean regression test used later in Phase 5.
trigger: n/a (rationale)
outcome: minimization is understood as feeding both hypothesis generation and the eventual regression test
notes: Rationale connecting Phase 2's output to Phases 3 and 5.
rationale: Supporting rationale, not independently actionable.

statement: Minimization is done when every remaining element is load-bearing — removing any one of them makes the loop go green.
trigger: minimizing the repro
outcome: a precise, testable stopping condition for minimization is applied
notes: Formal exit criterion for the minimize sub-step.
rationale: Exit condition for a sub-procedure of stage 20, not a separate top-level checkpoint.

statement: The actor must not proceed past Phase 2 until the bug has been both reproduced and minimized.
trigger: reproduction is confirmed but minimization is incomplete, or vice versa
outcome: the actor is blocked from Phase 3 until both conditions hold
notes: Ordering gate between stage 20 and stage 30.
rationale: Durable checkpoint/gate enforcing that reproduce-and-minimize both complete before hypothesis work starts.

statement: Before testing any of them, the actor generates 3-5 ranked hypotheses, because generating only one hypothesis anchors reasoning on the first plausible idea.
trigger: the bug is reproduced and minimized
outcome: a ranked, multi-hypothesis list exists before any hypothesis is tested
notes: Anti-anchoring rule with a concrete count (3-5).
rationale: Entry requirement and defining behavior of the third durable checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: generate and test a single leading hypothesis (rejected explicitly: anchoring risk)

statement: Each hypothesis must be falsifiable, stated in the form 'If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse'; if no prediction can be stated, the hypothesis is a vibe to be discarded or sharpened.
trigger: generating hypotheses
outcome: only falsifiable, prediction-bearing hypotheses survive into Phase 4
notes: A concrete falsifiability template and a discard rule for hypotheses that fail it.
rationale: Quality gate applied to each hypothesis within stage 30.

statement: The ranked hypothesis list should be shown to the user before testing begins, since users often re-rank instantly from domain knowledge or already-ruled-out hypotheses; this is a cheap checkpoint that should not block progress if the user is away.
trigger: hypotheses are ranked and falsifiable
outcome: the user gets a chance to re-rank or rule out hypotheses without blocking the actor if unavailable
notes: A non-blocking human checkpoint — consult if available, proceed if not.
rationale: A judgment-requiring, optional human-in-the-loop checkpoint inside stage 30, explicitly non-blocking.
alternatives_considered: require the user's sign-off before proceeding (rejected explicitly: 'Don't block on it')

statement: Each instrumentation probe in Phase 4 must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3, changing exactly one variable at a time.
trigger: hypotheses exist from Phase 3
outcome: instrumentation is targeted and interpretable rather than diffuse
notes: Discipline rule tying instrumentation to specific hypotheses.
rationale: Defines the fourth durable checkpoint's operating discipline.

statement: Instrumentation tool preference is ordered: debugger/REPL inspection where the environment supports it (one breakpoint beats ten logs), then targeted logs at boundaries that distinguish hypotheses, and never 'log everything and grep'.
trigger: choosing an instrumentation method
outcome: the least diffuse tool available is chosen first
notes: A ranked tool preference with an explicit anti-pattern.
rationale: Tool-selection guidance within the instrument stage.

statement: Every debug log must be tagged with a unique prefix (e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`) so cleanup at the end becomes a single grep; untagged logs survive cleanup, tagged ones die.
trigger: adding temporary debug logging
outcome: all temporary logging is grep-removable by construction
notes: A concrete, checkable convention that later feeds the Phase 6 cleanup checklist.
rationale: Deterministic convention applied within the instrument stage; its payoff is checked later in Phase 6.

statement: For performance regressions, logs are usually the wrong tool; instead the actor establishes a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan) and then bisects — measure first, fix second.
trigger: diagnosing a performance regression specifically
outcome: a measured baseline exists before any fix is attempted
notes: A conditional branch of the instrument stage specific to performance bugs.
rationale: Bug-class-specific instrumentation guidance inside stage 40.

statement: The regression test is written before the fix, but only if there is a correct seam for it.
trigger: a fix is about to be applied
outcome: test-first discipline is applied conditionally on seam availability
notes: Core Phase 5 rule, conditioned on seam correctness.
rationale: Defines the fifth durable checkpoint and its governing condition.

statement: A correct seam is one where the test exercises the real bug pattern as it occurs at the call site; a too-shallow seam (single-caller test for a multi-caller bug, a unit test that can't replicate the triggering chain) gives false confidence.
trigger: deciding whether a seam is adequate for a regression test
outcome: the actor distinguishes a load-bearing test seam from a misleading one
notes: Defines the judgment test for 'correct seam', directly reusing the seam vocabulary also central to the tdd skill.
rationale: Judgment criterion applied within stage 50; conceptually shared with tdd/SKILL.md's seam definition though not textually identical.

statement: If no correct seam exists, that absence is itself the finding: it must be noted as evidence that the codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down, and flagged for the next phase.
trigger: no correct test seam is available
outcome: the seam gap is recorded as a durable finding rather than silently skipped
notes: Converts a missing capability into a first-class, carried-forward finding.
rationale: Branch of stage 50 whose output feeds into the Phase 6 architectural recommendation.
alternatives_considered: silently skip the regression test with no record (rejected explicitly)

statement: When a correct seam exists, the procedure is: turn the minimized repro into a failing test at that seam, watch it fail, apply the fix, watch it pass, then re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original un-minimized scenario.

source.locator: Phase 5: procedure when a seam exists, lines 116-122

trigger: a correct seam has been identified
outcome: the fix is proven both at the minimal seam and against the original full scenario
notes: The five-step red-green-verify sequence, closing the loop back to Phase 1's original (non-minimized) scenario.
rationale: This is the operational content of the fifth checkpoint; five ordered sub-steps culminating in re-verification against the original scenario, which is exactly the kind of outcome an operator would want to see completed.

statement: Before declaring the diagnosis done, the actor must confirm: the original repro no longer reproduces, the regression test passes (or the seam absence is documented), all `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation is removed via a prefix grep, throwaway prototypes are deleted or clearly marked, and the correct hypothesis is stated in the commit/PR message for the next debugger.
trigger: a fix has been applied
outcome: a fixed set of closing conditions is verified before the diagnosis is considered complete
notes: The formal completion checklist for the sixth and final checkpoint.
rationale: This is the durable completion checkpoint of the whole workflow — an operator would care whether every item was verified before calling the bug closed.

statement: After the fix is in, the actor asks what would have prevented the bug; if the answer involves architectural change (no good test seam, tangled callers, hidden coupling) the actor hands off to the `/improve-codebase-architecture` skill with specifics, making the recommendation only after the fix — not before, since more is known by then.
trigger: the fix and cleanup checklist are complete
outcome: an architectural-improvement recommendation is optionally handed off to a separate workflow, timed deliberately after the fix
notes: References a skill (`/improve-codebase-architecture`) not present in the vendored corpus (not one of the 179 inventoried files) — the composition intent (hand off to an architecture-improvement workflow) is the durable behavior; the specific target skill name is an external reference that could not be verified against this snapshot.
rationale: Optional judgment-driven handoff at the close of the final stage; timing rule ('after the fix, not before') is the load-bearing part.
alternatives_considered: always hand off regardless of cause (rejected: only architecturally-caused bugs warrant it)

statement: The implement skill implements a piece of work described by the user against a spec or set of tickets.
trigger: the user hands over a spec or ticket set to implement
outcome: the implement workflow is entered
notes: Trigger/purpose of the workflow, minimal but explicit.
rationale: Recognizable trigger (a spec/ticket set), bounded outcome (implemented work, committed), and completion condition (commit) — matches §6.2's workflow test.
alternatives_considered: fold into the tdd workflow directly (rejected: implement composes tdd as one of several steps, it is not itself tdd)

statement: The implement skill disables automatic model-driven invocation (`disable-model-invocation: true`): it must be explicitly invoked by the user or coordinator, not triggered implicitly by the model recognizing the situation.
trigger: deciding whether to enter the implement workflow
outcome: the workflow only starts on explicit invocation, never silently inferred
notes: This is an invocation-policy attribute of the workflow entry itself (mirrored by the paired `agents/openai.yaml`'s `allow_implicit_invocation: false`, which is helper-evidence metadata for a different harness's display, not separately decomposed here).
rationale: This is a property of how the workflow may be entered (explicit-only), not a stage inside it; the ICM catalog needs an equivalent 'invocation policy' concept on the workflow entry to preserve this.
alternatives_considered: treat as a stage-level gate (rejected: it governs workflow entry, not an internal checkpoint)

statement: The implement workflow should use the tdd workflow where possible, at seams pre-agreed for testing.
trigger: implementation work is underway
outcome: test-first discipline (via the tdd workflow) governs how code seams get built
notes: Explicit composition: implement invokes tdd as a sub-procedure at agreed seams; textually references the seam vocabulary defined in tdd/SKILL.md.
rationale: This composes another named workflow (tdd) rather than defining new procedure — a synthesis-stage concern about how catalog entries reference each other.
alternatives_considered: always require tdd (rejected: 'where possible' implies a seam-availability condition, not an absolute)

statement: During implementation, typechecking and single test files should be run regularly, with the full test suite run once at the end.
trigger: implementation work is underway
outcome: fast, frequent local checks are interleaved with work, with one full-suite pass at the close
notes: A concrete verification cadence rule.
rationale: A meaningful durable checkpoint an operator would care about: whether typechecking/tests ran regularly and the full suite ran at the end, independent of the specific test runner used.
alternatives_considered: run the full suite continuously (rejected implicitly: too slow to run regularly; regular narrow checks plus one full pass is the stated cadence)

statement: Once implementation is done, the code-review skill/workflow is used to review the work.
trigger: implementation and verification are complete
outcome: the code-review workflow is invoked as the next composed step
notes: Explicit composition: implement invokes code-review as its review stage.
rationale: References another named workflow (code-review) as the review checkpoint rather than defining review procedure inline.

statement: The final step of implement is to commit the work to the current branch.
trigger: the work has been implemented, verified, and reviewed
outcome: the change is committed to the current branch
notes: Terminal checkpoint of the workflow.
rationale: A durable, measurable checkpoint (committed or not) closing the workflow.

statement: no-mistakes is vendored for reference only in a worker's context: workers and remediation loops must never invoke `no-mistakes axi run`, only the Sergeant coordinator owns every no-mistakes gate, and a worker running inside a brief-guided worktree may read the skill to understand the contract but must not execute it, per an AGENTS.md hard-error rule ('Workers and remediation loops never run no-mistakes').
trigger: an actor other than the coordinator considers running the shipping-gate pipeline
outcome: the pipeline is invoked only by the coordinator; a worker context is refused this action
notes: This is an authority/role boundary: which actor context is permitted to invoke an external, side-effecting command. It is stated as a hard error tied to AGENTS.md, i.e. treated as a repo-wide invariant, not a per-workflow rule.
rationale: Attempted at three lower rungs (see engine_gap) and each fails because the current engine has no first-class notion of actor role/authority that a runtime mechanism can enforce; only prose can express it today.
alternatives_considered: AGENTS.md-style repository invariant instructing every actor not to run the command (attempted; source's own primary mechanism)
author every worker-facing workflow/stage to omit any reference to the no-mistakes command (attempted in spirit by this being a 'reference only' skill)
wrap the underlying command behind a helper script that checks the caller's role before executing (not attempted in the source; considered here as a lower rung)

engine_gap.behavior: Only a coordinator-context actor may invoke the no-mistakes shipping-gate pipeline; a worker or remediation-loop context must be structurally prevented from invoking it, not merely instructed not to.
engine_gap.evidence: reference/sergeant-upstream/.agents/skills/no-mistakes/SKILL.md lines 8-13 (quote_hash sha256:f8d4fed6d3fdda65e670c17256ed90243d38bcc5fa0f697a96b3f2b3ab80d568): the banner states the restriction is 'a hard error per AGENTS.md' and vendors the skill 'for reference only' precisely so a worker can understand but not execute it.
lower_rungs_attempted: Repository-wide instruction/invariant (AGENTS.md rule quoted verbatim in the banner) telling every actor never to run the command from a worker context.
Workflow-authoring discipline: keep the command's invocation entirely out of any worker-facing workflow/stage content so a worker actor is never even prompted to run it.
A deterministic helper/wrapper script that gates the underlying command behind a role check before executing it.
engine_gap.why_each_fails: The AGENTS.md instruction only binds an actor that reads and honors it; nothing in the current engine distinguishes a 'coordinator' execution from a 'worker' execution at the runtime level, so a differently-prompted or careless worker-context actor can still issue the command and nothing structurally stops it. Keeping the command out of worker-facing workflow content prevents accidental invocation via authored content, but does not prevent an actor from invoking the underlying command directly (e.g. via a shell tool) since the runtime does not restrict which external commands a given actor context may execute. A role-checking helper script requires the runtime to expose a trustworthy, unforgeable 'which role is this execution' identity for the helper to check; the current engine has no such actor-role identity to hand the helper.
engine_gap.minimum_capability: The runtime must own and expose an authoritative actor-role/authority identity per execution (e.g. distinguishing a coordinator-owned Work from a dispatched worker context), and must be able to gate specific external command invocations by that identity so a worker-context execution attempting the restricted command is refused by the runtime itself, not merely discouraged by instructions.
engine_gap.acceptance_test: Given a worker-context execution that attempts to invoke the shipping-gate command, the runtime refuses the invocation (or the tool call is blocked/denied) and emits an observable refusal event distinguishable from a normal command failure; the same invocation from a coordinator-context execution succeeds.

statement: no-mistakes is a local gate that validates code changes through a fixed pipeline of stages — intent, rebase, review, test, document, lint, push, PR, CI — before they reach the configured push target.
trigger: a change is ready to be validated for shipping
outcome: the change passes through the named pipeline stages before reaching the push target
notes: Names the pipeline's constituent stages in order.
rationale: This describes the shape of an entire external pipeline (intent→rebase→review→test→document→lint→push→PR→CI) that the coordinator drives as one composed validation workflow; each named stage is a candidate durable checkpoint of that composed workflow.
alternatives_considered: treat the whole pipeline as one indivisible stage of a larger workflow (rejected: each named phase — review, test, lint, etc. — is independently a decision point with its own gate/outcome, per the rest of this document)

statement: When the user invokes /no-mistakes, the actor reports the outcome at the end; if the user asks for something specific (e.g. 'skip the lint step'), the actor translates that request into the matching `axi run` flag itself (e.g. `--skip=lint`), consulting `axi run --help` for available flags.
trigger: the user invokes the no-mistakes command, optionally with a specific request
outcome: user intent is translated into concrete CLI flags rather than passed through unparsed
notes: Translation responsibility placed on the actor, with a documented discovery mechanism (`--help`) rather than a fixed flag list memorized in the skill.
rationale: Judgment step (translating natural language into flags) at the entry of the workflow; the help-output discovery pattern is itself flagged by the source inventory as directly relevant to the proposal's harness-capability-probe design (see bin/_sgt-intent.sh, P6).

statement: no-mistakes has two invocation modes: validate-only, where the user's changes are already committed and the actor just validates and reports; and task-first, where the actor first carries out the described task, then validates the result.
trigger: the user invokes /no-mistakes with or without a task description
outcome: the correct one of two distinct procedures is followed based on whether a task was given
notes: The branching condition for the whole workflow's entry.
rationale: A durable, judgment-requiring branch point at the very start of the workflow — which of the two procedures applies changes everything downstream.
alternatives_considered: a single invocation mode covering both cases (rejected: the two modes have materially different preconditions — commit-first vs. do-the-work-first)

statement: In task-first mode, before changing or committing anything the actor inspects `git status`, preserves unrelated pre-existing uncommitted changes, and when committing, commits only the changes belonging to the user's task.
trigger: task-first mode is entered
outcome: only the task's own changes are committed; unrelated pre-existing changes survive untouched
notes: A scope-isolation rule protecting the user's other in-progress work.
rationale: A meaningful checkpoint: whether scope was checked and preserved before any mutation is exactly the kind of state an operator would want verified.

statement: The actor makes the changes the task describes and commits them on a feature branch; if the user is on the repository's default branch, a feature branch must be created first, because the gate validates committed history on a non-default branch.
trigger: the task's changes have been made
outcome: the work lands as a commit on a non-default feature branch before validation can proceed
notes: A hard precondition (non-default branch) enforced proactively at this step rather than merely checked later.
rationale: Durable checkpoint: committed-on-a-feature-branch is a concrete, verifiable state the pipeline depends on.

statement: The actor then validates, passing the user's task text as `--intent` verbatim, enriched with the decisions and tradeoffs made while doing the work.
trigger: the task is committed on a feature branch
outcome: validation begins with an intent string that captures the user's goal plus the actor's own tradeoff decisions
notes: Ties task-first mode back into the shared intent-passing rule (see NM17/NM18).
rationale: Entry into the shared validate-and-decide checkpoint, common to both invocation modes.

statement: The work to be validated must already be committed on a branch; the gate validates committed history, not the uncommitted working tree.

source.locator: Before you start: committed work, lines 54-55

trigger: preparing to run the pipeline
outcome: uncommitted changes are never what gets validated
notes: First of four stated preconditions.
rationale: A precondition checked before entering the validate stage.

statement: The actor must be on a feature branch, not the repository's default branch, before running the pipeline.

source.locator: Before you start: feature branch, lines 56-56

trigger: preparing to run the pipeline
outcome: the pipeline is never run directly against the default branch
notes: Second precondition.
rationale: Precondition check before the validate stage; overlaps with NM06's proactive branch creation.

statement: The repository must already be initialized with `no-mistakes init` before the pipeline can be run.

source.locator: Before you start: initialized repo, lines 57-57

trigger: preparing to run the pipeline
outcome: an uninitialized repository cannot be validated until `no-mistakes init` has been run
notes: Third precondition.
rationale: Precondition check before the validate stage.

statement: The daemon must have a runnable configured pipeline agent — a supported native agent binary, the `agent: cursor` ACP alias, or an explicit `acp:<target>` via `acpx` — since the invoking actor is the AXI driver, not an implicit pipeline-agent backend; without one, the run fails before its first step and `no-mistakes doctor` reports the configuration problem.

source.locator: Before you start: pipeline agent, lines 58-62

trigger: preparing to run the pipeline
outcome: the run fails fast with a diagnosable configuration error rather than partway through, if no pipeline agent is configured
notes: Fourth precondition; names the doctor-style diagnostic escape hatch.
rationale: Precondition check before the validate stage, with a named remediation path (`no-mistakes doctor`).

statement: If any precondition is unmet, `axi run` returns an `error:` with the exact command to fix it, which the actor reads and acts on (committing work, or creating a branch); an uninitialized repo needs `no-mistakes init` first, and a broken `no-mistakes` command itself needs `no-mistakes doctor`.
trigger: a precondition check fails
outcome: the actor is given, and follows, a concrete remediation command rather than guessing
notes: Establishes that precondition failures are self-describing and actionable.
rationale: Failure-handling behavior of the precondition-check step.

statement: Before starting, the actor runs `no-mistakes axi` (home view); if it shows an active run on the current branch, the actor inspects it with `axi status`, and if it is parked at a gate, drives it with `axi respond`.
trigger: about to start a new validation
outcome: an existing in-flight run on the same branch is discovered and handled instead of a redundant new run being started
notes: First check in a small state machine for reconciling with any pre-existing run.
rationale: A durable, state-dependent checkpoint: whether a prior run exists on this branch changes the entire next action.

statement: An in-flight run is reattached by re-running `no-mistakes axi run` when it still matches the current HEAD, either as the submitted head or the current pipeline head.
trigger: an active run exists on the current branch and matches HEAD
outcome: the same run is continued rather than a new one started
notes: Idempotent-resume rule keyed on HEAD matching.
rationale: Sub-rule of the home-view reconciliation checkpoint.

statement: `axi abort` is only used when the actor means to discard the current run before starting over; it is a between-runs action, never a way to take over or bypass a gate while a run is still going.
trigger: considering whether to abort an active run
outcome: abort is used only to intentionally discard a run, never to sidestep an active gate
notes: A hard usage restriction preventing abort from being used as a gate-bypass mechanism.
rationale: Constrains legal actor actions during the validate stage.

statement: If the home view shows an active run on another branch, that run is left alone and the actor starts validation for the current branch independently.
trigger: an active run exists but on a different branch than the current one
outcome: the other branch's run is left untouched while the current branch's validation proceeds independently
notes: Isolation rule between concurrent per-branch runs.
rationale: Final branch of the home-view reconciliation checkpoint.

statement: Starting a run requires `--intent`: what the user set out to accomplish, in their own terms — not a description of the diff or changed files — since no-mistakes uses it verbatim rather than inferring it from local agent transcripts, which the source calls slower and flakier.
trigger: starting a validation run
outcome: the run is anchored to a stated human goal rather than an inference over the diff
notes: Defines what `--intent` is and is not, and why it's required verbatim rather than inferred.
rationale: Required input to the validate stage's entry action; judgment is needed to state the goal correctly.

statement: The intent should err toward completeness, not brevity, since the review step uses it to tell a deliberate decision from a mistake: it should capture the user's goal, the specific decisions and tradeoffs made, constraints ruled in or out, and anything explicitly requested that might otherwise look surprising in the diff.
trigger: composing the `--intent` text
outcome: a rich enough intent is provided that the review step can distinguish deliberate choices from mistakes
notes: Explains the downstream consequence (review-step accuracy) of a thin intent, motivating the completeness rule.
rationale: Quality bar for the required intent input.

statement: Starting the run (`no-mistakes axi run --intent "..."`) blocks until the first decision point or the end.
trigger: the run is started
outcome: the actor's call does not return until a gate or a terminal outcome is reached
notes: Basic synchronous-call semantics of the pipeline driver.
rationale: Defines the blocking contract of the core validate loop's driving action.

statement: `axi run` and every `axi respond` block synchronously and each step can take several minutes, so a single call may not return for a while; that is normal, requires a long timeout, and must not be interrupted or re-issued because it seems slow — progress can be checked separately via `axi status` without disturbing the run.
trigger: a pipeline call is in flight and appears slow
outcome: the actor waits out the call (backgrounding it if needed) rather than cancelling or re-issuing it, using `axi status` to observe progress
notes: A hard patience rule with an explicit non-disruptive observability escape hatch.
rationale: Operating discipline for the actor while the run is blocked mid-call.
alternatives_considered: cancel and retry when a call seems slow (rejected explicitly)

statement: The `awaiting_agent: parked <duration>` field on status output means the run is parked at a gate waiting for `axi respond`; the field is observability only — it does not change gate resolution, auto-resume the run, or make `--yes` the default.
trigger: reading `axi status` output on a parked run
outcome: the field is correctly understood as informational, not actionable on its own
notes: Explicitly disclaims side-effects the field might be mistaken for having.
rationale: Interpretation rule for one status field.

statement: While a step is `running` or `fixing`, `axi status` may include an `active_steps` table with `active_for`, `last_activity`, a native `agent_pid` when a subprocess agent is running, and the current round (e.g. `round 1`, `auto-fix 1/3`, `fix 2`); a `last_activity` prefixed `quiet` means no step log or agent-lifecycle activity has arrived for longer than `step_quiet_warning`.
trigger: monitoring an active step via `axi status`
outcome: the actor can read detailed liveness/progress information about the currently running step
notes: Describes the observable shape of in-progress step state.
rationale: Observability detail for the validate stage.

statement: A `quiet` last_activity is a liveness clue only, not permission to cancel, rerun, or edit the worktree.
trigger: observing a quiet, possibly-stalled step
outcome: the actor treats apparent staleness as information, not authorization to intervene
notes: Explicit restriction preventing the actor from over-reacting to an ambiguous liveness signal.
rationale: Constrains actor behavior in response to the active_steps observability data.
alternatives_considered: treat 'quiet' as a stall and intervene (rejected explicitly)

statement: A `gate:` object means the pipeline is waiting on the actor; its findings table has `id`, `severity`, `file`, `description`, and an `action` classifying it as `auto-fix` (mechanical/low-risk, actor may authorize on their own judgment), `no-op` (informational, nothing to do), or `ask-user` (challenges the user's deliberate intent or touches product behavior — a decision only the user can make).
trigger: the pipeline returns a `gate:` object
outcome: each finding is classified into one of three action categories that determine who may decide it
notes: The central decision-authority classification of the whole review-decision model.
rationale: This is the durable checkpoint's core decision structure: what an operator/actor must resolve at a gate, and the authority boundary (auto-fix/no-op decidable by the actor, ask-user reserved for the user) between them.

statement: Review auto-fix is disabled by default (`auto_fix.review: 0`; a repo- or global-level `auto_fix.review > 0` override re-enables it), so blocking and ask-user review findings park for actor decision rather than being silently self-fixed; other steps such as test and lint may still auto-fix within the pipeline and re-run before ever gating.
trigger: the review step produces findings
outcome: review findings default to parking for a decision rather than silent auto-fixing, unlike some other pipeline steps
notes: A specific, overridable default that changes how much actor judgment is required at the review gate versus other steps.
rationale: Configuration-dependent behavior of the gate-decision checkpoint.

statement: At a gate the actor chooses exactly one response: `--action approve` (accept as-is and continue), `--action fix --findings <ids> [--instructions "..."]` (have the pipeline fix specific findings and continue), or `--action skip` (skip this step).
trigger: deciding how to respond to a gate
outcome: one of three defined actions is chosen and issued via `axi respond`
notes: The fixed response vocabulary for resolving any gate.
rationale: Defines the actor's available moves at the gate checkpoint.

statement: While a run is active the actor must never fix findings by editing the code directly — the pipeline owns both findings and fixes, and the actor's job at a gate is to decide and respond via `--action fix`, which has the pipeline apply the fix and re-review; for the same reason the actor must not `abort` or `rerun` mid-run to go fix something themselves, even a real bug in their own code, since that discards the pipeline's in-flight work and forces full re-validation.
trigger: a gate finding looks fixable to the actor
outcome: the actor routes every fix through the pipeline's own fix mechanism instead of editing the worktree or restarting the run
notes: A hard ownership boundary: the pipeline, not the actor, mutates code during an active run.
rationale: Constrains legal actor actions while the validate stage's loop is in progress.
alternatives_considered: let the actor apply the fix directly and continue (rejected explicitly: 'the pipeline owns both the findings and the fixes')

statement: Each `axi respond` blocks until the next `gate:`, `checks-passed` decision point, or final outcome.
trigger: the actor has responded to a gate
outcome: the call does not return until the next decision point is reached
notes: Same blocking contract as the initial run call, restated for respond.
rationale: Blocking-call semantics for the loop's iteration step.

statement: `--add-finding '<json>'` (used with `--action fix`) folds a finding the actor spotted themselves — one the pipeline did not surface — into the current fix round, as a JSON finding object.
trigger: the actor notices a problem the pipeline's gate did not surface
outcome: the actor-observed problem is included in the same fix round as pipeline-surfaced findings
notes: Extension mechanism letting the actor inject findings into the pipeline's own fix flow.
rationale: Optional flag on the respond action.

statement: `--step <name>` responds to a specific step instead of the one currently awaiting approval, and is rarely needed since omitting it answers the active gate.
trigger: responding to a gate
outcome: responses target the active gate by default, with an explicit override available
notes: Minor targeting flag, default behavior stated explicitly.
rationale: Optional flag on the respond action.

statement: `checks-passed` means the change is validated and CI is green but the PR is not yet merged; the actor is done driving the pipeline and should tell the user the PR is ready to review and merge (link is in the `help` line) without waiting for the merge, since no-mistakes keeps monitoring the PR in the background until merged, closed, or idle-timed-out.
trigger: the pipeline reaches the checks-passed outcome
outcome: the actor stops driving and hands the merge decision to the user, while the pipeline's own monitor continues in the background
notes: Defines one of the workflow's terminal-for-the-actor outcomes and the handoff it implies.
rationale: A named, durable terminal state of the composed pipeline, with its own follow-on behavior (background PR monitoring).

statement: `passed` means the changes cleared the gate and the PR was merged or closed.
trigger: the pipeline reaches the passed outcome
outcome: the workflow's fully-terminal success state is reached
notes: The other success terminal outcome.
rationale: A named durable terminal state.

statement: `failed` or `cancelled` mean the change did not clear the gate; the actor reads the output, fixes whatever is pointed at (a failing test, lint error, or a skipped finding), commits the fix on the same feature branch, and drives the pipeline again with a fresh `axi run --intent` or `no-mistakes rerun`; the actor must not leave the user at a failed outcome without either retrying or explaining what blocks it.
trigger: the pipeline reaches a failed or cancelled outcome
outcome: the actor either retries after a concrete fix or explicitly explains the blocker to the user — never silence
notes: Names the two failure terminal states and mandates a non-silent recovery path.
rationale: A named durable terminal state with a mandatory follow-up behavior; also establishes that a fresh run or `rerun` is a between-runs action, correct only after a terminal outcome.
alternatives_considered: leave the user without explanation on failure (rejected explicitly)

statement: Before any post-pipeline local commit or fresh run, the actor reads the structured `branch_sync` object returned by AXI home/status/drive results, and runs `no-mistakes axi sync` only when its `next_action.code` is `sync`.
trigger: about to make a local commit or start a fresh run after a pipeline interaction
outcome: branch synchronization is checked and, if indicated, performed before any local action
notes: A precondition gate on a class of post-pipeline actor actions, keyed to a structured field rather than actor judgment.
rationale: A durable checkpoint governing branch-state consistency between the actor's local git operations and the pipeline's own branch ownership.

statement: A guarded sync may be a strict fast-forward or a content-equivalent diverged advance that anchors the pre-sync head before moving the branch with reset semantics; genuine divergence stays blocked.
trigger: performing `axi sync`
outcome: only fast-forward or provably content-equivalent advances are applied automatically; real divergence is refused
notes: Defines the safety envelope of the automated sync operation.
rationale: Behavior detail of the sync sub-action, protecting against silent history loss.

statement: If `next_action.code` is `continue_active_run`, the pipeline still owns the branch: the actor runs the reported command, keeps driving the active run, and makes no local follow-up commits.
trigger: branch_sync reports continue_active_run
outcome: the actor defers entirely to the still-active pipeline run rather than acting locally
notes: One branch of the branch_sync decision.
rationale: Conditional handling within the reconcile checkpoint.

statement: If `next_action.code` is `recover_custody`, a terminal run left unpublished pipeline commits preserved in the local gate; the actor runs `no-mistakes axi sync --recover` to return custody and fast-forward to the preserved head, or `no-mistakes rerun` to resume validating it instead.
trigger: branch_sync reports recover_custody
outcome: the actor either recovers the preserved pipeline commits or resumes validation of them, never discards them silently
notes: Names the recovery path for a specific failure-adjacent state (terminal run, unpublished commits).
rationale: Conditional recovery handling within the reconcile checkpoint; directly analogous to sergeant-rs's own recovery/ambiguity-fails-closed philosophy.

statement: A dirty or diverged worktree makes recovery refuse with explicit choices; `--keep-local` keeps the actor's current head while the preserved commits stay anchored under `refs/no-mistakes/recover/<run>`; when synchronization is blocked the actor must process the structured state rather than improvising reset, stash, merge, rebase, force, or branch replacement.
trigger: synchronization or recovery is blocked by worktree state
outcome: the actor uses the offered structured choices rather than any manual git surgery
notes: A hard prohibition on manual git intervention when the pipeline's own recovery mechanism reports a blocked state.
rationale: Constrains actor behavior at a blocked-recovery checkpoint.
alternatives_considered: improvise a manual git fix (reset/stash/merge/rebase/force/branch-replace) (rejected explicitly)

statement: After synchronization, the actor commits the follow-up on top and re-runs `no-mistakes axi run --intent "..."` with the original user intent, which preserves every prior gate-fix commit regardless of its configured subject.
trigger: synchronization has completed
outcome: follow-up work is committed on top and validation resumes with the original intent, without losing prior pipeline commits
notes: Closes the branch_sync procedure with a concrete next action.
rationale: Final step of the branch_sync handling sequence.

statement: The CI step deliberately keeps watching the PR after checks pass, so `axi run` returns `checks-passed` as soon as checks are green rather than blocking on the human merge; the actor must never poll or re-run waiting for the merge.
trigger: checks have passed but the PR is not yet merged
outcome: the actor does not poll or loop waiting for a human merge; the pipeline's own monitor covers it
notes: Explains why checks-passed is a legitimate stopping point for the actor.
rationale: Behavior/rationale tied to the checks-passed outcome.
alternatives_considered: poll for merge completion (rejected explicitly)

statement: A PR that falls behind the default branch or hits a merge conflict after checks pass needs no command from the actor and must never be hand-rebased: the still-running CI monitor detects an actual conflict, rebases onto the base, resolves it, and re-pushes itself; a merely-behind-but-clean PR needs nothing since the platform merges it; the one exception is when the monitor is no longer running (PR closed, run aborted/superseded, idle-timed-out, or auto-fix attempts exhausted), in which case the actor recovers with `no-mistakes rerun`, which cancels the stale monitor and re-runs the full pipeline including a deterministic rebase step; `no-mistakes axi run` must not be used to refresh a still-active PR, since after checks-passed it just reattaches to the running monitor without rebasing.
trigger: a PR has passed checks and later drifts behind the base or conflicts
outcome: drift/conflict is resolved by the pipeline's own live monitor automatically; the actor intervenes only when that monitor has stopped, and then via `rerun`, never a hand-rebase
notes: A detailed automatic-recovery rule with one explicit escape hatch and an explicit prohibition on the wrong recovery command.
rationale: Conditional post-checks-passed handling, distinguishing when the actor must act from when the pipeline handles it unattended.
alternatives_considered: hand-rebase the PR directly (rejected explicitly)
use `no-mistakes axi run` to refresh a still-active PR (rejected explicitly: reattaches without rebasing)

statement: On a successful outcome (`checks-passed` or `passed`), the actor closes the loop with the user by summarizing what happened during the pipeline concisely and readably — what was validated and what was found — and if the output includes a `fixes` table, explicitly acknowledges and lists each fix the pipeline made that the actor's original change missed.
trigger: the pipeline reaches a successful terminal or near-terminal outcome
outcome: the user receives an honest, itemized summary including fixes the pipeline had to make
notes: Closing communication requirement, including an explicit honesty rule about pipeline-made fixes.
rationale: A durable, user-facing completion checkpoint of the whole workflow.

statement: A gate whose findings are all `auto-fix` or `no-op` may be driven on the actor's own judgment, but any `ask-user` finding is a decision that belongs to the user because it challenges their deliberate intent or changes product behavior; the actor must not approve, fix, or skip it on their own — it must stop and bring it to the user first.
trigger: a gate contains at least one ask-user finding
outcome: the actor defers that specific decision to the user instead of resolving it independently
notes: The core authority-boundary rule for the highest-stakes finding category.
rationale: Judgment-requiring escalation branch of the gate-decision checkpoint (NM24); the actor must recognize which category a finding falls into and act accordingly.
alternatives_considered: resolve ask-user findings using the actor's own judgment (rejected explicitly)

statement: Each `ask-user` finding is relayed to the user verbatim (id, file, full description, not paraphrased or pre-judged); the actor asks how they want to proceed and translates their decision into the matching `respond` call (`--action fix` with `--instructions`, `--action approve`, or `--action skip`).
trigger: an ask-user finding has been identified
outcome: the user's own decision, not the actor's interpretation of it, determines the eventual respond call
notes: The concrete relay-and-translate procedure for the escalation.
rationale: Operational detail of the escalation branch; a needs_input-style human-in-the-loop interaction, currently representable through direct user conversation within the actor stage.

statement: `--yes` is the user's standing consent to drive every gate unattended: it treats every actionable finding (auto-fix and ask-user alike) as consent to fix, selects every current finding for one fix round, accepts the resulting fix review, and approves gates with only no-op findings; it should only be used when the user has asked to drive the whole run without checking back, and it is the sole exception to the ask-user escalation rule (NM43).
trigger: the user has given explicit standing consent to run unattended
outcome: ask-user findings are resolved automatically instead of stopping to ask, but only under this explicit consent flag
notes: Defines the single override to the otherwise-mandatory human escalation rule, and the scope of what that override authorizes.
rationale: A consent-gated mode switch on the gate-decision checkpoint; requires the actor to have obtained clear consent before use.

statement: A fixed set of read-only or narrowly-scoped inspection/control commands exists: `axi` (home view), `axi status` (full detail plus cached branch_sync), `axi sync --check` (verify an offered plan), `axi sync` (apply an offered plan), `axi sync --recover` (return custody), `axi logs --step <name> --full`, `axi abort` (current-branch run), `axi abort --run <id>` (specific run, works outside its worktree).
trigger: inspecting or lightly controlling pipeline state outside the main gate loop
outcome: the actor has a fixed vocabulary of inspection/control commands available
notes: A reference command table, invoked as needed rather than as sequential steps.
rationale: Deterministic command reference used throughout the validate/reconcile stages rather than tied to one checkpoint; candidate shared helper/context content for any workflow driving this pipeline.

statement: Output is TOON (`key: value` pairs, `name[N]{cols}:` tables, `help[N]:` hints); a non-terminal run object may include `awaiting_agent: parked <duration>`; a `running`/`fixing` run may include an `active_steps` table; the bottom `help` list names next commands; errors print as `error: ...` with a `help` list; exit codes are `0` (success/no-op/normal gate), `1` (failed/cancelled terminal outcomes), `2` (bad usage).

source.locator: Output format and exit codes, lines 264-271

trigger: parsing any no-mistakes CLI output
outcome: output is interpreted according to a fixed, documented structural format and exit-code contract
notes: The structural output contract the actor relies on throughout the workflow.
rationale: A stable output-format convention used across every stage's interaction with the underlying pipeline command; not itself a checkpoint.

statement: In a worked gate example, the actor decides each row by its `action` column — auto-fix findings can be authorized directly, ask-user findings must be escalated — while a terminal state instead shows `outcome: <checks-passed|passed|failed|cancelled>` with no findings table; field names and exact columns can vary by step and version, so the actor must read the actual `findings` header rather than assume a fixed layout.
trigger: reading a concrete gate or outcome response
outcome: the actor parses the response structurally (by header) rather than assuming a hardcoded schema, and applies the auto-fix/ask-user distinction per row
notes: Combines a worked example with an explicit forward-compatibility warning about schema drift.
rationale: Reinforces NM24's per-row action classification with a concrete example and a parsing-robustness caveat.

statement: The tdd workflow triggers when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions 'red-green-refactor', or wants integration tests.
trigger: the user asks for test-first work or names red-green-refactor/integration tests
outcome: the tdd workflow is entered
notes: Entry trigger for the workflow.
rationale: Recognizable trigger, bounded outcome (a passing test-first implementation of one slice), and completion condition — matches §6.2's workflow test.

statement: TDD is the red-to-green loop; this skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping (what a good test is, where tests go, anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop), and every section applies on every cycle, consulted before and during the loop, not after.
trigger: running any red-green cycle
outcome: the same quality rules are applied on every cycle, not retrofitted afterward
notes: States the workflow's scope and that its rules are continuously applicable, not a one-time setup checklist.
rationale: Frames how the whole workflow's sub-rules apply (continuously, every cycle) rather than describing a single checkpoint.

statement: When exploring the codebase for tdd, the actor should read CONTEXT.md (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area being touched.
trigger: beginning to write a test in an unfamiliar area of the codebase
outcome: test names and vocabulary align with the project's own domain language
notes: Textually near-identical to diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md's CONTEXT.md/ADR instruction (DB02) — strong evidence this is a shared, cross-workflow context-loading convention rather than workflow-local prose duplicated by coincidence.
rationale: Same convention appears verbatim in spirit in another workflow (diagnose-bug); candidate for a single shared context/instruction rather than two independent copies.
alternatives_considered: workflow-local instruction only (rejected: duplicated near-verbatim in diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md, suggesting a shared convention)

statement: Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details; code can change entirely while tests shouldn't, and a good test reads like a specification that survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

source.locator: What a good test is, lines 14-14

trigger: writing or evaluating a test
outcome: the test is judged by whether it exercises the public interface and would survive an internal refactor
notes: The core quality definition the rest of the skill (seams, anti-patterns) operationalizes.
rationale: A stable definitional standard applied throughout every cycle of the loop, not a single checkpoint; reinforced with concrete examples in the paired tests.md file (TS01-TS06).
alternatives_considered: stable operating invariant at repo level (considered, but scoped specifically to how tests are written within this workflow)

statement: A seam is the public boundary a test is written at: the interface where behavior is observed without reaching inside; tests live at seams, never against internals.
trigger: deciding where a test should attach to the code
outcome: tests are anchored at public interfaces exclusively
notes: Defines the central vocabulary term ('seam') that recurs in diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md's Phase 5 (DB27) as well.
rationale: A definitional term used as shared vocabulary across at least two workflows in this partition (tdd and diagnose-bug).

statement: Test seams must be pre-agreed: before writing any test the actor writes down the seams under test and confirms them with the user, and no test is written at an unconfirmed seam, since agreeing seams up front is how testing effort lands on critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.
trigger: about to write the first test of a cycle
outcome: the seam is explicitly confirmed with the user before any test is written
notes: A mandatory human-consent checkpoint gating the start of every red-green cycle.
rationale: A meaningful durable checkpoint: whether seams were agreed with the user before writing tests is exactly the kind of state an operator would want verified, and requires judgment (which seams matter) plus explicit consent.
alternatives_considered: let the actor pick seams unilaterally (rejected explicitly: 'confirm them with the user')

statement: The actor asks the user: 'What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?'
trigger: confirming seams with the user
outcome: a concrete, repeatable question is used to elicit the seam agreement
notes: The literal prompt used for the seam-confirmation checkpoint.
rationale: Concrete phrasing supporting TD06's checkpoint; not itself a separate checkpoint.

statement: An implementation-coupled test mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (e.g. querying the database instead of using the interface); the tell is that it breaks on refactor even though behavior hasn't changed.
trigger: writing or reviewing a test
outcome: tests that would break on a pure refactor are recognized and avoided
notes: First named anti-pattern with its diagnostic tell; directly reinforced with worked examples in tests.md (TS03/TS04/TS05).
rationale: A named anti-pattern checked throughout every cycle, not a single checkpoint.

statement: A tautological test recomputes the expected value the way the code does (mirrored logic, a hand-derived snapshot, a self-equal constant), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code; expected values must come from an independent source of truth (a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec).
trigger: writing or reviewing a test's expected value
outcome: expected values are drawn from an independent source, never recomputed via the same logic as the implementation
notes: Second named anti-pattern, reinforced with a worked before/after example in tests.md (TS06).
rationale: A named anti-pattern checked throughout every cycle.

statement: Horizontal slicing (writing all tests first, then all implementation) verifies imagined behavior rather than user-facing behavior, tests the shape of things rather than real behavior, goes insensitive to real changes, and commits to test structure before the implementation is understood; work should instead proceed in vertical slices — one test, one implementation, repeat — each test a tracer bullet responding to what the last cycle taught.
trigger: planning how to sequence tests versus implementation across a feature
outcome: work proceeds one test-then-implementation slice at a time rather than in bulk-test, bulk-implement phases
notes: Third named anti-pattern; this one is structural/sequencing rather than about a single test's shape, and directly motivates TD12's 'one slice at a time' rule of the loop.
rationale: Governs sequencing across the whole loop rather than one test's construction; closely tied to the loop rules (TD11-TD13).
alternatives_considered: bulk-write tests then bulk-implement (rejected explicitly as the horizontal-slicing anti-pattern)

statement: Red before green: the failing test is written first, then only enough code is written to pass it, without anticipating future tests or adding speculative features.
trigger: starting a red-green cycle
outcome: the test exists and fails before any implementation code is written, and the implementation is minimal
notes: The foundational ordering rule of the loop, plus a scope-minimization rule ('only enough code').
rationale: The defining durable checkpoint of the loop: whether red came before green, and whether the implementation stayed minimal, is exactly what an operator would want verified per cycle.
alternatives_considered: write speculative/future-proofed code beyond the current failing test (rejected explicitly)

statement: One slice at a time: one seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
trigger: running a red-green cycle
outcome: each cycle's scope is bounded to exactly one seam/test/implementation triple
