notes: Bounds the granularity of each loop iteration.
rationale: Scope discipline for the red-green-cycle stage.

statement: Refactoring is not part of the red-green loop; it belongs to the review stage (the code-review skill), not the implementation cycle.
trigger: tempted to refactor mid-cycle
outcome: refactoring is deferred to a separate review stage rather than folded into the red-green cycle
notes: An explicit boundary between tdd and code-review, naming code-review by name — direct composition/ordering evidence between the two workflows in this partition.
rationale: This is a boundary rule about which workflow owns which concern (tdd owns red-green; code-review owns refactor/review), informing how the two catalog entries compose rather than defining new procedure of its own.
alternatives_considered: fold refactoring into the red-green loop (rejected explicitly)

statement: Mocking is reserved for system boundaries only: external APIs (payment, email, etc.), databases (sometimes, prefer a test DB), time/randomness, and the file system (sometimes).
trigger: deciding what to mock while writing a test
outcome: only genuine system-boundary dependencies are considered mockable
notes: Positive list defining the scope of legitimate mocking.
rationale: Reference content (a boundary definition) consulted while writing any test, not a checkpoint itself; reinforced across the whole loop.

statement: The actor must not mock their own classes/modules, internal collaborators, or anything they control.
trigger: deciding what to mock while writing a test
outcome: internal code is never mocked, only genuine external boundaries
notes: Negative list paired with MK01, and the concrete instance of the 'implementation-coupled' anti-pattern (TD08) as applied to mocking specifically.
rationale: Same status as MK01 — durable reference content for the write-test checkpoint.

statement: At system boundaries, dependencies should be designed for mockability via dependency injection: external dependencies are passed in rather than created internally by the function that uses them.
trigger: designing code that touches a system boundary
outcome: the boundary dependency is injectable, making it independently mockable in tests
notes: A design rule that exists specifically to make MK01's boundary-mocking practical.
rationale: Design guidance supporting testability at boundaries; applies whenever boundary code is authored, not a single checkpoint.

statement: SDK-style interfaces (one specific function per external operation) are preferred over one generic fetcher function with conditional logic, because each function is then independently mockable.
trigger: designing an interface to an external system
outcome: each external operation gets its own specific, independently-mockable function rather than a shared generic call
notes: A second, more specific design rule for boundary interfaces.
rationale: Design guidance supporting testability, applied whenever boundary interfaces are authored.
alternatives_considered: a single generic fetcher with conditional logic (rejected explicitly, with a labeled BAD example in source)

statement: The SDK-style approach means each mock returns one specific shape, there is no conditional logic in test setup, it's easier to see which endpoints a test exercises, and there is type safety per endpoint.
trigger: n/a (rationale for MK04)
outcome: the SDK-style design choice is understood in terms of its four concrete testing benefits
notes: Enumerated benefits supporting MK04's rule.
rationale: Supporting rationale for MK04, not independently actionable.

statement: Good tests are integration-style: they test through real interfaces, not mocks of internal parts.
trigger: writing a test
outcome: the test exercises real collaborators through the public interface rather than mocking internals
notes: Restates TD04/TD08's core standard as the file's opening rule, with a worked code example following in source.
rationale: Reinforces TD04/TD08 with a concrete worked example; same non-checkpoint status.

statement: Good tests are characterized by testing behavior users/callers care about, using only the public API, surviving internal refactors, describing WHAT not HOW, and asserting one logical thing per test.
trigger: evaluating whether a test is well-formed
outcome: a test can be checked against five concrete characteristics
notes: A five-point checklist operationalizing 'good test'.
rationale: Checklist reference content used throughout the write-test checkpoint.

statement: A bad, implementation-detail test is one coupled to internal structure.
trigger: writing or reviewing a test
outcome: coupling to internal structure is recognized as a defect
notes: Restates TD08's definition as the file's negative-case heading, with a worked BAD example following.
rationale: Reinforces TD08 with a worked negative example.

statement: Red flags for a bad test include: mocking internal collaborators, testing private methods, asserting on call counts/order, breaking on refactor without a behavior change, a test name describing HOW instead of WHAT, and verifying through external means instead of the interface.
trigger: evaluating whether a test is well-formed
outcome: a test can be checked against six concrete red flags to catch implementation-coupling
notes: A six-point checklist operationalizing the implementation-coupled anti-pattern (TD08).
rationale: Checklist reference content, an operational elaboration of TD08.

statement: Verifying through a side channel (e.g. querying the database directly after calling `createUser`) is a bad-test pattern; the good version verifies the same outcome through the public interface itself (e.g. calling `getUser` after `createUser` and asserting on its result).
trigger: verifying a side effect of an operation under test
outcome: the effect is verified by calling back through the same public interface, never by reaching into a side channel like the database directly
notes: A concrete before/after example of the 'side channel' implementation-coupled anti-pattern named abstractly in TD08.
rationale: Worked example elaborating TD08's 'side channel' tell.
alternatives_considered: verify via direct data-store inspection (rejected explicitly, labeled BAD in source)

statement: A tautological test recomputes the expected value using the same logic the implementation uses (e.g. re-running the same `reduce` the function under test performs) so it passes by construction; the fix is to assert against an independent, known literal expected value instead.
trigger: writing an assertion's expected value
outcome: the expected value is an independently known literal, never a value recomputed via the implementation's own logic
notes: A concrete before/after example of the tautological-test anti-pattern named abstractly in TD09.
rationale: Worked example elaborating TD09's definition.
alternatives_considered: recompute the expected value via the same algorithm under test (rejected explicitly, labeled BAD in source)
